claim: Cyanogenic glucosides are among the most widespread defense chemicals of plants.
source: Cyanogenic glucosides are among the most widespread defense chemicals of plants.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about plant defense chemistry.

claim: Upon plant tissue disruption, cyanogenic glucosides are hydrolyzed to a reactive hydroxynitrile that releases toxic hydrogen cyanide (HCN).
source: Upon plant tissue disruption, these glucosides are hydrolyzed to a reactive hydroxynitrile that releases toxic hydrogen cyanide (HCN).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of cyanogenic glucoside activation.

claim: Many mite and lepidopteran species can thrive on plants defended by cyanogenic glucosides.
source: Yet many mite and lepidopteran species can thrive on plants defended by cyanogenic glucosides.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about herbivore-plant interactions.

claim: The enzyme that detoxifies HCN to β-cyanoalanine in arthropods has remained enigmatic.
source: The nature of the enzyme known to detoxify HCN to β-cyanoalanine in arthropods has remained enigmatic.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study, based on existing literature.

claim: The gene encoding the HCN detoxification enzyme is a member of the cysteine synthase family horizontally transferred from bacteria to phytophagous mites and Lepidoptera.
source: Phylogenetic analysis showed that the gene is a member of the cysteine synthase family horizontally transferred from bacteria to phytophagous mites and Lepidoptera.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript (Figure 2) and multiple lines of genomic evidence.

claim: The recombinant mite enzyme had both β-cyanoalanine synthase and cysteine synthase activity.
source: The recombinant mite enzyme had both β-cyanoalanine synthase and cysteine synthase activity but enzyme kinetics showed that cyanide detoxification activity was strongly favored.
evidence: This is supported by experimental enzyme activity assays shown in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: Enzyme kinetics showed that cyanide detoxification activity was strongly favored over cysteine synthase activity.
source: The recombinant mite enzyme had both β-cyanoalanine synthase and cysteine synthase activity but enzyme kinetics showed that cyanide detoxification activity was strongly favored.
evidence: This is supported by the specificity constant ratio (CAS/CYS = 33.7) shown in Table 1.

claim: An ancient horizontal transfer of a gene originally involved in sulfur amino acid biosynthesis in bacteria was co-opted by herbivorous arthropods to detoxify plant produced cyanide.
source: Our results therefore suggest that an ancient horizontal transfer of a gene originally involved in sulfur amino acid biosynthesis in bacteria was co-opted by herbivorous arthropods to detoxify plant produced cyanide.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis, enzyme activity data, and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: More than 2500 plant species are known to synthesize cyanogenic glucosides and cyanolipids as phytoanticipins.
source: Cyanogenesis is one of the most ancient and widespread of these defenses, and more than 2500 plant species are known to synthesize cyanogenic glucosides and cyanolipids as phytoanticipins (constitutive defense compounds present in the plant prior to herbivore attack).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature, as indicated by the context.

claim: Upon tissue disruption by herbivore feeding, cyanogenic glucosides are degraded by plant β-glucosidases and α-hydroxynitrile lyases, resulting in the release of toxic hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and other toxic products such as their aglycones.
source: Upon tissue disruption by herbivore feeding, cyanogenic glucosides are degraded by the plant β-glucosidases and α-hydroxynitrile lyases, which results in the release of toxic hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and other toxic products such as their aglycones (Gleadow and Woodrow, 2002; Poulton, 1990; Spencer, 1988; Zagrobelny et al., 2004; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Released cyanide is a potent inhibitor of the mitochondrial respiratory chain.
source: The released cyanide is a potent inhibitor of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and has a disruptive effect on various metabolic pathways (Solomonson, 1981), thus providing a broad defense against generalist herbivores.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cyanide has a disruptive effect on various metabolic pathways.
source: The released cyanide is a potent inhibitor of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and has a disruptive effect on various metabolic pathways (Solomonson, 1981), thus providing a broad defense against generalist herbivores.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cyanide provides a broad defense against generalist herbivores.
source: The released cyanide is a potent inhibitor of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and has a disruptive effect on various metabolic pathways (Solomonson, 1981), thus providing a broad defense against generalist herbivores.
evidence: This is an inference based on the toxic properties of cyanide and established knowledge.

claim: Arthropods have evolved several mechanisms to overcome plant cyanogenesis.
source: In their arms race with plants, arthropods have evolved several mechanisms to overcome plant cyanogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant-herbivore coevolution.

claim: Insect lepidopteran specialists sequester ingested cyanogenic glucosides in their own defense against predators.
source: A well-documented case of co-evolution is found in insect lepidopteran specialists that sequester the ingested cyanogenic glucosides in their own defense against predators.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lepidopteran defense strategies.

claim: Some species such as burnet moths (Zygaenidae) not only sequester, but also synthesize cyanogenic compounds de novo by convergent evolution of the biosynthetic pathways.
source: Remarkably, cyanogenic compounds have become so crucial for some species such as burnet moths (Zygaenidae) that they not only sequester, but also synthesize these compounds de novo by convergent evolution of the biosynthetic pathways (Jensen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jensen et al., 2011.

claim: In animals, HCN is thought to be detoxified by two main pathways.
source: In animals, HCN is thought to be detoxified by two main pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cyanide detoxification in animals.

claim: The enzyme rhodanese converts cyanide into thiocyanate, but this biochemical reaction is not very common and thought to be inefficient.
source: The enzyme rhodanese converts cyanide into thiocyanate, but this biochemical reaction is not very common and thought to be inefficient (Beesley et al., 1985; Davis and Nahrstedt, 1985; Long and Brattsten, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The conversion of HCN and cysteine into β-cyanoalanine and sulfide has been suggested as the main detoxification pathway in arthropods.
source: Alternatively, the conversion of HCN and cysteine into β-cyanoalanine and sulfide has been suggested as the main detoxification pathway in arthropods (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Several biochemical surveys show a correlation between β-cyanoalanine synthesis and HCN exposure in lepidopteran species tolerant to HCN.
source: This is supported by several biochemical surveys showing a correlation between β-cyanoalanine synthesis and HCN exposure in lepidopteran species tolerant to HCN (Meyers and Ahmad, 1991; Stauber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of HCN into β-cyanoalanine in arthropods has not been identified prior to this study.
source: However, the enzyme that catalyzes this crucial reaction in arthropods has not been identified to date.
evidence: This reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The conversion of HCN into β-cyanoalanine by an enzyme called β-cyanoalanine synthase (CAS) has been best studied in bacteria and plants.
source: The conversion of HCN into β-cyanoalanine by an enzyme called β-cyanoalanine synthase (CAS) has been best studied in bacteria and plants that need to protect themselves from HCN during the synthesis of cyanogenic glucosides or ethylene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CAS enzymes in bacteria and plants.

claim: Enzymes responsible for CAS activity also have cysteine synthase activity (CYS).
source: The enzymes responsible for CAS activity also have cysteine synthase activity (CYS) and are referred to as CYS or CAS depending on their substrate specificity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the dual activity of these enzymes.

claim: CYS catalyzes the conversion of O-acetylserine into cysteine, an essential final step in the cysteine biosynthesis pathway unique for plants and bacteria.
source: CYS catalyzes the conversion of O-acetylserine into cysteine, an essential final step in the cysteine biosynthesis pathway unique for plants and bacteria (Bonner et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Animals synthesize cysteine by a different pathway and use related enzymes such as cystathionine-β-synthase (CBS) and cystathionine-γ-lyase (CGL).
source: Animals synthesize cysteine by a different pathway and use related enzymes such as cystathionine-β-synthase (CBS) and cystathionine-γ-lyase (CGL), which form together with CAS and CYS a group of pyridoxal-5′-phosphate dependent enzymes (Finkelstein et al., 1988; Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Tetranychus urticae is one of the most polyphagous arthropod pests known to date.
source: This species is one of the most polyphagous arthropod pests known to date, and feeds on more than 1100 plant species from more than 140 plant families, including many cyanogenic plants (Grbic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Tetranychus urticae feeds on more than 1100 plant species from more than 140 plant families, including many cyanogenic plants.
source: This species is one of the most polyphagous arthropod pests known to date, and feeds on more than 1100 plant species from more than 140 plant families, including many cyanogenic plants (Grbic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A spider mite strain was transferred from acyanogenic bean plants (Phaseolus vulgaris) to a cultivar of Phaseolus lunatus containing high levels of cyanogenic glucosides and allowed to adapt for more than 30 generations.
source: We transferred a spider mite strain reared on acyanogenic bean plants (Phaseolus vulgaris) to a cultivar of Phaseolus lunatus containing high levels of well characterized cyanogenic glucosides such as linamarin and lotaustralin (Ballhorn et al., 2006; Jones, 1998; Wybouw et al., 2012) and allowed the strain to adapt to this host plant for more than 30 generations.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Phaseolus lunatus contains high levels of well characterized cyanogenic glucosides such as linamarin and lotaustralin.
source: We transferred a spider mite strain reared on acyanogenic bean plants (Phaseolus vulgaris) to a cultivar of Phaseolus lunatus containing high levels of well characterized cyanogenic glucosides such as linamarin and lotaustralin (Ballhorn et al., 2006; Jones, 1998; Wybouw et al., 2012) and allowed the strain to adapt to this host plant for more than 30 generations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Only a limited set of 28 genes was found differentially expressed between the parental and adapted lines (absolute fold change ≥2, Benjamini-Hochberg corrected p-value <0.05).
source: In contrast to the broad response previously detected after host plant changes from Fabaceae to Solanaceae and Brassicaceae (Grbic et al., 2011; Dermauw et al., 2013), only a limited set of 28 genes (absolute fold change ≥2, Benjamini-Hochberg corrected p-value <0.05) was found differentially expressed between the parental and adapted lines (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Within the differentially expressed genes, 18 had an increased expression in the adapted line, while 10 exhibited a lower expression.
source: Within this small set of genes, 18 had an increased expression in the adapted line, while 10 exhibited a lower expression.
evidence: This is based on microarray data analysis.

claim: The most differentially expressed genes after transfer to cyanogenic lima bean encode closely related, small cytoplasmic proteins of unknown function.
source: The most differentially expressed genes after transfer to cyanogenic lima bean encode closely related, small cytoplasmic proteins of unknown function.
evidence: This is based on analysis of microarray data.

claim: Among the genes with increased expression were three cytochrome P450 genes, known to respond readily to host plant changes.
source: Among the genes with an increased expression were three cytochrome P450 genes, known to respond readily to host plant changes (Grbic et al., 2011; Dermauw et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on microarray data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A gene (tetur10g01570, Tu-CAS) encoding a predicted cytosolic protein with high similarity to bacterial cysteine synthases was identified among genes with increased expression.
source: Moreover, we identified a gene (tetur10g01570, Tu-CAS) encoding a predicted cytosolic protein with high similarity to bacterial cysteine synthases (Conserved Domain Database (CDD): COG0031).
evidence: This is based on microarray data and sequence analysis.

claim: Close homologues of Tu-CAS were only detected in two closely related tetranychid mites within chelicerates.
source: Within chelicerates, we only detected close homologues of Tu-CAS in two closely related tetranychid mites.
evidence: This is based on sequence searches in genomic and transcriptomic databases.

claim: CAS genes were identified in Tetranychus evansi and Panonychus citri.
source: By sequencing PCR amplicons (see below, this section) and a tBLASTn-search in a published transcriptome (Liu et al., 2011), CAS genes were identified in Tetranychus evansi and Panonychus citri, respectively.
evidence: This is based on PCR sequencing and database searches.

claim: A tBLASTn-search in published genomes of mesostigmatid mites and of ticks (Metastigmata) did not reveal homologues.
source: A tBLASTn-search in published genomes of mesostigmatid mites and of ticks (Metastigmata) did not reveal homologues (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on database searches.

claim: Close homologues of Tu-CAS were detected in lepidopteran genomes (Bombyx mori, Danaus plexippus, Heliconius melpomene, Manduca sexta and Plutella xylostella).
source: Broadening the search to arthropods by tBLASTn-searches in NCBI databases and additional arthropod genome portals (Supplementary file 2), we only detected close homologues of Tu-CAS in lepidopteran genomes (Bombyx mori, Danaus plexippus, Heliconius melpomene, Manduca sexta and Plutella xylostella) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on database searches and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Tu-CAS showed on average 75% similarity with lepidopteran protein sequences.
source: On average, Tu-CAS showed 75% similarity with lepidopteran protein sequences, and genes encoding these proteins were intronless in both mites and insects.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Genes encoding CAS proteins were intronless in both mites and insects.
source: On average, Tu-CAS showed 75% similarity with lepidopteran protein sequences, and genes encoding these proteins were intronless in both mites and insects.
evidence: This is based on genomic sequence analysis.

claim: A total of 20 (complete and partial) homologous sequences were identified in arthropods by searching additional NCBI EST-databases and published lepidopteran transcriptomes.
source: By searching additional NCBI EST-databases and published lepidopteran transcriptomes, a total of 20 (complete and partial) homologous sequences were identified in arthropods.
evidence: This is based on database searches.

claim: Phylogenetic reconstruction indicated that arthropod CAS homologous sequences might be monophyletic and were embedded with high node support within bacterial cysteine synthase sequences, indicative of a horizontal gene transfer.
source: A phylogenetic reconstruction of these arthropod proteins with CYS, CAS and CBS enzymes of plants, fungi, oomycetes, bacteria and Metazoa indicated that these homologous arthropod sequences might be monophyletic. They were embedded with high node support within bacterial cysteine synthase sequences, indicative of a horizontal gene transfer (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The most closely related sequences to arthropod CAS are from bacteria that belong to the α- and β-Proteobacteria, two of which are Methylobacterium species.
source: The most closely related sequences are from bacteria that belong to the α- and β-Proteobacteria, two of which are Methylobacterium species, free-living epiphytic bacteria known to establish endophytic colonies.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Methylobacterium species are free-living epiphytic bacteria known to establish endophytic colonies.
source: The most closely related sequences are from bacteria that belong to the α- and β-Proteobacteria, two of which are Methylobacterium species, free-living epiphytic bacteria known to establish endophytic colonies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Methylobacterium species.

claim: Methylobacterium species are reported to be transferred from the plant to phytophagous insects and to survive inside arthropod hosts.
source: These species are reported to be transferred from the plant to phytophagous insects and to survive inside arthropod hosts (Kutschera, 2007; Rampelotti-Ferreira et al., 2010), facilitating a potential horizontal gene transfer.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The transfer of Methylobacterium from plants to insects facilitates a potential horizontal gene transfer.
source: These species are reported to be transferred from the plant to phytophagous insects and to survive inside arthropod hosts (Kutschera, 2007; Rampelotti-Ferreira et al., 2010), facilitating a potential horizontal gene transfer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biology of Methylobacterium and HGT mechanisms.

claim: Proteobacteria are known endosymbionts of arthropods and often reside in the reproductive organs for vertical transmission to following generations.
source: Alternatively, Proteobacteria are known endosymbionts of arthropods and often reside in the reproductive organs for vertical transmission to following generations (Wernegreen, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The intimate relationship between Proteobacteria and arthropods makes successful horizontal gene transfer more likely to occur.
source: Because of this intimate relationship, successful horizontal gene transfer is more likely to occur (Hotopp, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on HGT mechanisms.

claim: The mite and insect CAS sequences formed a branch in bacterial cysteine synthase enzymes, some of which have documented dual CYS and CAS activities.
source: The mite and insect sequences formed a branch in bacterial cysteine synthase enzymes, some of which have documented dual CYS and CAS activities (Omura et al., 2003) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and supported by a citation.

claim: The arthropod protein sequences and their closest bacterial homologues shared a unique 9 amino acid insertion not present in cysteine synthases of other organisms.
source: The arthropod protein sequences and their closest bacterial homologues shared a unique 9 amino acid insertion not present in cysteine synthases of other organisms, but the residues known to be crucial for substrate and cofactor binding in plants and bacteria showed conservation (Bonner et al., 2005; Yi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The residues known to be crucial for substrate and cofactor binding in plants and bacteria showed conservation in arthropod CAS sequences.
source: The arthropod protein sequences and their closest bacterial homologues shared a unique 9 amino acid insertion not present in cysteine synthases of other organisms, but the residues known to be crucial for substrate and cofactor binding in plants and bacteria showed conservation (Bonner et al., 2005; Yi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis and supported by citations.

claim: The lysine residue (Lys95) that forms a Schiff base linkage to the cofactor pyridoxal-5′-phosphate was conserved in arthropods.
source: The lysine residue (Lys95, Glycine max CAS numbering, Yi et al., 2012) that forms a Schiff base linkage to the cofactor pyridoxal-5′-phosphate was also conserved in arthropods (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tu-CAS is located on a 3 Mb large scaffold (scaffold 10) and is flanked by typical eukaryotic genes, tetur10g01550 and tetur10g01580.
source: Tu-CAS is located on a 3 Mb large scaffold (scaffold 10) and is flanked by typical eukaryotic genes, tetur10g01550 and tetur10g01580.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both genes flanking Tu-CAS (tetur10g01550 and tetur10g01580) contain introns with splice sites confirmed by EST or RNA-seq data.
source: Both genes contain introns with splice sites confirmed by EST or RNA-seq data (Grbic et al., 2011, GenBank: LIBEST_025606, Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on genomic and transcriptomic data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Tetur10g01580 encodes a nudix hydrolase highly similar to other arthropod nudix hydrolases.
source: Tetur10g01580 encodes a nudix hydrolase (CDD: cl00447) highly similar to other arthropod nudix hydrolases (BLASTp hits with E-value <1e−45).
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity searches.

claim: Remapping of T. urticae Sanger reads and examination of Illumina read coverage in two re-sequenced strains revealed no inconsistencies in the Tu-CAS region.
source: First, we remapped the T. urticae Sanger reads used for the genome assembly of the London strain of T. urticae (Grbic et al., 2011) and examined the Illumina read coverage of the Tu-CAS region in two re-sequenced strains (EtoxR and Montpellier) that are geographically distinct from the London strain (Grbic et al., 2011; Van Leeuwen et al., 2012). Neither Sanger nor Illumina-reads revealed any inconsistencies in the Tu-CAS region in any of these strains (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on genomic read mapping analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: A 6 kb genomic region bracketing Tu-CAS with the surrounding spliced genes was amplified using a PCR approach.
source: Second, using a PCR approach, we amplified a 6 kb genomic region bracketing Tu-CAS with the surrounding spliced genes (tetur10g01550 and tetur10g01580, Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A 6 kb region was amplified in the closely related spider mite T. evansi using a similar strategy.
source: Using a similar strategy we also amplified a 6 kb region in the closely related spider mite T. evansi (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and a nucleotide dot plot between the amplified region of these two species showed clear synteny and the absence of discontinuity around the CAS gene (Figure 4).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A nucleotide dot plot between the amplified regions of T. urticae and T. evansi showed clear synteny and the absence of discontinuity around the CAS gene.
source: Using a similar strategy we also amplified a 6 kb region in the closely related spider mite T. evansi (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and a nucleotide dot plot between the amplified region of these two species showed clear synteny and the absence of discontinuity around the CAS gene (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The GC/GC3 content of Tu-CAS was most similar to the GC/GC3 content of genes from the T. urticae genome, and quite distinct from the GC/GC3 content of genes from the three annotated bacterial genomes in the closest sister clade.
source: Indeed, the GC/GC3 content of Tu-CAS was most similar to the GC/GC3 content of genes from the T. urticae genome, and quite distinct from the GC/GC3 content of genes (including the CYS/CAS genes) from the three annotated bacterial genomes in the closest sister clade to the apparent monophyletic arthropod clade (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on codon usage analysis shown in Figure 5, indicating amelioration.

claim: Tu-CAS is a sequence integrated in the genome of T. urticae and does not represent bacterial contamination.
source: Taken together, these data provide strong evidence that Tu-CAS is a sequence integrated in the genome of T. urticae and does not represent bacterial contamination.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of genomic evidence (read mapping, PCR, synteny, amelioration).

claim: Recombinantly expressed Tu-CAS in E. coli was obtained in mg quantities after affinity purification.
source: In order to functionally test whether arthropod enzymes are active and still able to catalyze both reactions after horizontal gene transfer, we recombinantly expressed Tu-CAS in Escherichia coli and obtained mg quantities after affinity purification.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for protein production.

claim: Biochemical assays confirmed that Tu-CAS catalyzes both CYS and CAS reactions.
source: Subsequent biochemical assays confirmed that Tu-CAS catalyzes both reactions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on enzyme activity assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: The CAS/CYS ratio of the specificity constants was 33.7, showing that CAS activity was strongly favored over CYS activity.
source: The CAS/CYS ratio of the specificity constants was 33.7, showing that CAS activity was strongly favored over CYS activity (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on enzyme kinetics data shown in Table 1.

claim: The preferred CAS activity of Tu-CAS is typical of known plant CAS enzymes and clearly different from CYS enzymes.
source: This preferred CAS activity is typical of known plant CAS enzymes and clearly different from CYS enzymes (Table 1; Yamaguchi et al., 2000; Wada et al., 2004; Bogicevic et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison of enzyme kinetics data in Table 1 with literature values.

claim: Enzymatic activity of Tu-CAS was dependent on pyridoxal-5′-phosphate as a cofactor.
source: Enzymatic activity was dependent on pyridoxal-5′-phosphate as a cofactor, and the substrate-dependent formation of β-cyanoalanine was further confirmed by thin layer chromatography (TLC) and LC-MS (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on enzyme activity assays.

claim: The substrate-dependent formation of β-cyanoalanine was confirmed by thin layer chromatography (TLC) and LC-MS.
source: Enzymatic activity was dependent on pyridoxal-5′-phosphate as a cofactor, and the substrate-dependent formation of β-cyanoalanine was further confirmed by thin layer chromatography (TLC) and LC-MS (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on analytical chemistry data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The very high sequence similarity between Tu-CAS and the lepidopteran proteins strongly suggests that the lepidopteran proteins can catalyze the same two reactions (cyanide detoxification and cysteine synthesis).
source: The very high sequence similarity between Tu-CAS and the lepidopteran proteins strongly suggests that the lepidopteran proteins can catalyze the same two reactions (cyanide detoxification and cysteine synthesis) and that these proteins are responsible for the known wide occurrence of CAS activity in lepidopteran species (Witthohn and Naumann, 1987; Meyers and Ahmad, 1991; Stauber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence similarity and known CAS activity in Lepidoptera.

claim: The lepidopteran CAS proteins are responsible for the known wide occurrence of CAS activity in lepidopteran species.
source: The very high sequence similarity between Tu-CAS and the lepidopteran proteins strongly suggests that the lepidopteran proteins can catalyze the same two reactions (cyanide detoxification and cysteine synthesis) and that these proteins are responsible for the known wide occurrence of CAS activity in lepidopteran species (Witthohn and Naumann, 1987; Meyers and Ahmad, 1991; Stauber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence similarity and literature on CAS activity in Lepidoptera.

claim: The ability to detoxify HCN plays a crucial ecological role in arthropods and is thought to have allowed the exploitation of cyanogenic plants.
source: In arthropods, the ability to detoxify HCN plays a crucial ecological role and is thought to have allowed the exploitation of cyanogenic plants by circumventing the toxic effects of HCN.
evidence: This is an inference based on ecological and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: The two-spotted spider mite increases transcript levels of a horizontally transferred β-cyanoalanine synthase upon adaptation on cyanogenic bean.
source: We have shown here that the two-spotted spider mite increases transcript levels of a horizontally transferred β-cyanoalanine synthase upon adaptation on cyanogenic bean.
evidence: This is based on microarray data showing differential expression.

claim: Phylogenetic evidence alone does not constitute strong evidence for horizontal gene transfer.
source: Phylogenetic evidence alone does not constitute strong evidence for horizontal gene transfer (HGT), because in the absence of introns in the sequence, a contamination of the mite genome sequence with a sequence from a bacterial symbiont or commensal cannot be excluded.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of phylogenetic evidence for HGT.

claim: The results of mite genomic analysis, codon amelioration, synteny and genomic PCR, combined with the phylogenetic evidence, unambiguously prove that T. urticae CAS has a bacterial origin and was laterally transferred and incorporated into the mite genome prior to the divergence in the Tetranychidae.
source: However, the results of mite genomic analysis, codon amelioration, synteny and genomic PCR, combined with the phylogenetic evidence, unambiguously prove that T. urticae CAS has a bacterial origin and was laterally transferred and incorporated into the mite genome prior to the divergence in the Tetranychidae.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: A homologous lateral gene transfer has also occurred in Lepidoptera.
source: A homologous lateral gene transfer has also occurred in Lepidoptera (Figure 2) raising the question of the time and number of HGT events needed to explain the phylogenetic pattern of distribution of the CYS/CAS genes.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The hypothesis of a single HGT to a common ancestor of mites and insects, followed by selective losses, is not parsimonious due to the numerous losses that would be required.
source: The broad sampling of arthropod species that revealed the absence of any CYS/CAS-like sequence (even as a distant recognizable trace) argues against the origin of the gene in the common ancestor of tetranychid mites and Lepidoptera, followed by multiple independent losses. These losses would have to be numerous: seven in the hexapods (Trichoptera, Diptera, Hymenoptera, Coleoptera/Strepsiptera, Hemiptera/Heteroptera/Thysanoptera/Phthiraptera, Orthoptera, Odonata/Ephemeroptera) and six further in other arthropods (Copepoda/Branchiopoda, Myriapoda, Aranea, Scorpiones, Metastigmata and Mesostigmata). This figure of 13 losses is an absolute minimum that implies that the loss occurred each time at the origin of the lineage, that is before any speciation beyond the point of coalescence. A loss later in the history of each lineage would rapidly increase the total number of losses. We strongly believe that this hypothesis is not parsimonious, and therefore that there was no CYS/CAS gene in the common ancestor of mites and Lepidoptera.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic reasoning and parsimony analysis.

claim: Two HGT events might have occurred (one to a mite ancestor, one to a lepidopteran ancestor) or a single HGT from a donor bacterial species, followed by a transfer between a mite and a lepidopteran.
source: (b) Alternatively, two HGT events might have occurred (one to a mite ancestor, one to a lepidopteran ancestor) or (c) a single HGT from a donor bacterial species, followed by a transfer between a mite and a lepidopteran.
evidence: These are alternative hypotheses proposed based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The apparent monophyly of the arthropod CAS gene may be due to the fact that both the mite and the insect gene came from very closely related bacteria not represented in the phylogenetic tree.
source: The apparent monophyly of the arthropod CAS gene may be due to the fact that both the mite and the insect gene came from very closely related bacteria, but these bacteria are not represented in the tree.
evidence: This is speculation about the phylogenetic pattern.

claim: The transfer from a lepidopteran to mite is improbable, because the mite sequence would branch with the closest relative to the lepidopteran donor, rather than being basal.
source: The transfer from a lepidopteran to mite is improbable, because the mite sequence would branch with the closest relative to the lepidopteran donor, rather than being basal.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic reasoning.

claim: The authors favor the hypothesis of two HGT events, with a very old transfer to an ancestral lepidopteran, and a second transfer to an ancestral mite.
source: We therefore favor hypothesis (b), with a very old transfer to an ancestral lepidopteran, and a second transfer to an ancestral mite.
evidence: This is the authors' preferred hypothesis based on the available evidence.

claim: The absence of a CAS enzyme in Mesostigmata (typically parasitic and predatory mites) and Metastigmata (ticks) suggests transfer occurred after the split of Prostigmata in the Lower Devonian about 400 MYA.
